summary: Zur Mang Khenpo Pema Namgyal studied under Shenphen Nangwa and Pema Wangchok Gyelpo.
pad+ma la studied under Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche and Dudjom Rinpoche.

A scholar in Sinology, Buddhist studies, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, Édouard Chavannes studied at the ENS, Collège de France, and INALCO under teachers including the Marquis d'Hervey de Saint-Denys and Maurice Jametel. He was a professor at the Collège de France (1893–1918).

Active in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Indology, Édouard Huber studied at the University of Paris, École nationale des langues orientales vivantes, and Collège de France, including under Sylvain Lévi and Johann Baptist Schibenegg. He directed a department at EFEO (1901–1905).

Specializing in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology, Émile Benveniste studied at EPHE and the University of Paris under Antoine Meillet, Joseph Vendryes, and Sylvain Lévi. He held chairs at EPHE (1927–1969) and the Collège de France (1937–1969).
A scholar of philosophy, Émile Chartier studied at Lycée Pierre-Corneille (~1881–1886) and École Normale Supérieure (~1889–1892).

Specializing in history, archaeology, and linguistics, Émile Chatelain studied at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1874–1877). He later served at the École française de Rome (1876–1877) and the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1881–1925).

A scholar in religious studies and sociology, Émile Durkheim studied at ENS, University of Bordeaux, and Leipzig University under Wilhelm Wundt. He held academic posts at the University of Bordeaux (1887–1902), EPHE (1905), and the University of Paris (professor in 1902).

Specializing in Indology and Buddhist studies, Émile Senart studied at the University of Munich and the University of Göttingen under Theodor Benfey. He later served as professor at the Collège de France and president of the Société Asiatique (1908–1928).

An Indology and linguistics scholar, Émile-Louis Burnouf studied at ENS, University of Paris, and École française d'Athènes under Jean-Louis Burnouf and Eugène Burnouf. He held posts at the University of Nancy (1854–1867) and directed the École française d'Athènes (1867–1875).
Specializing in Indology and linguistics, Émilie Aussant studied under Georges-Jean Pinault and held a post at Paris Diderot University (attested 2014).

A scholar in Sinology, history, and archaeology, Étienne Balazs earned his doctorate under Otto Franke (1923–1930). He later worked as a CNRS senior researcher (1949) and held a professorship at the University of Paris/Sorbonne (~1955–1963).

Specializing in Buddhist studies and Indology, Étienne Lamotte studied at KU Leuven, Sapienza, EPHE, and the Sorbonne under Sylvain Lévi and Louis de La Vallée Poussin. He served as a professor at KU Leuven and Catholic University of Louvain (1932–1974).
Specializing in linguistics, history, and archaeology, Étienne Marc Quatremère studied under Antoine-Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. He held a post at the Collège de France from 1819 to 1857.

Working in Buddhist studies and philosophy, Ñāṇavīra Thera graduated from Magdalene College (1938) and served in the Royal Artillery and Intelligence Corps (1939–1945). He later studied under traditional teachers Nyanatiloka Mahathera and Pelene Siri Vajiragnana.

A Buddhist studies practitioner, Ösel Tendzin studied at Fordham University and under Satchidananda Saraswati and Chögyam Trungpa. He became executive vice president of Vajradhatu in 1973 and succeeded Trungpa in 1987.

A Buddhist studies scholar and monk, Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu studied at Oberlin College (~1967–1971) and trained under Fuang Jotiko (~1976–1986). He founded the Metta Forest Monastery, where he has served as abbot since 1993.
